messages.subject: betabinomial and linear separation
parts:
I run into the same error as in the example below when trying to fit a model with a large number of fixed interaction effects.  I suspect that this is caused by too many parameters making some predicted values (the mean of the beta distribution for p) numerically equal to 0 or 1 such that either alpha or beta of the beta-distribution takes a value of zero and the beta-function no longer can be evaluated.  But the probabilities of such observations should go to one as the corresponding predicted values goes to either 0 or 1 so this should not cause any error.

> x <- 0:9
> y <- rep(c(0,1),each=5)
> summary(inla(y~x,data=data.frame(y,x),fam="betabinomial",Ntrials=1))

I run into the same error as in the example below when trying to fit a model with a large number of fixed interaction effects.  I suspect that this is caused by too many parameters making some predicted values (the mean of the beta distribution for p) numerically equal to 0 or 1 such that either alpha or beta of the beta-distribution takes a value of zero and the beta-function no longer can be evaluated.  But the probabilities of such observations should go to one as the corresponding predicted values goes to either 0 or 1 so this should not cause any error.

In the example, the priors are the only thing pulling the posterior means for the linear predictor 
away from +/- Inf, so if the priors aren't strong enough, then numerical problems should be 
expected. It should be possible to detect this to avoid a crash, but the true result would not 
necessarily be sensible.

> x <- 0:9
> y <- rep(c(0,1),each=5)

In the example above, things as expected don't crash if increasing the precision of the prior for the fixed effects, but I find it strange that different estimates are produced if using a binomial likelihood instead (which should be equivalent to the betabinomial for Ntrials=1):

The betabinomial model has a hierarchical parameter structure (logit-normal for dispersion & 
conditionally beta for p), which is not equivalent to the binomial prior (logit-normal for p) for any 
value of Ntrials.  Normally, this probably would not be noticeable for Ntrials=1, but since the 
example data gives a degenerate ML estimate, the prior will here have a strong effect on the 
posterior.

Finn

messages.author: f66907f526d3c7bf
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] betabinomial and linear separation
parts:
You can't even estimate over-dispersion when Ntrials=1 (see Chapter 4 of McCullagh & Nelder, 1989, for example), so is this so surprising? In effect the overdispersion adds error, so by forcing it into the model you are saying that there is more noise, and hence less signal. I assume the difference in estimates is because the priors are relatively tight (you have a prior standard deviation of 5.8), so the beta-binomial model doesn't have enough information to push the intercept close to -20.

Bob

parts:
Sure, I know that for Ntrials=1 one cannot estimate overdispersion since the distribution of the data in this case do not depend on the overdispersion parameter of the betabinomial (denoted rho = 1/(alpha + beta +1) in inla).  So, as long as rho is independent of other parameters in the prior (which it is), the posterior for rho should be equal to the prior, and the posterior for other parameters should be identical to the results produced if using a binomial likelihood instead.  So this is why the example results are unexpected also in the degenerate case - the prior for everything else (the regression intercept and slope) are identical in the two cases.

In any case, my main concern was the problem with predicted values becoming numerically equal to 0 or 1 which appears to cause the crash.  This can easily occur if the response is always zero for some level of a factor in the model (or it can occur in less obvious ways involving some linear combination of covariates).  While parameter estimates obtained in such cases not necessarily can be trusted, it may still be of interest to fit an overparameterized model like this, for example, to assess goodness of fit of some simpler model.

Jarle

messages.author: afb003e064114795
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] betabinomial and linear separation
parts:
On 27 Nov 2014, at 15:20, Jarle Tufto <jarle...@gmail.com> wrote:

Sure, I know that for Ntrials=1 one cannot estimate overdispersion since the distribution of the data in this case do not depend on the overdispersion parameter of the betabinomial (denoted rho = 1/(alpha + beta +1) in inla).  So, as long as rho is independent of other parameters in the prior (which it is), the posterior for rho should be equal to the prior, and the posterior for other parameters should be identical to the results produced if using a binomial likelihood instead.

No, that reasoning is incorrect. The prior in the betabinomial model is not equivalent to the prior in the binomial model; they imply different data distributions, so the results should not be expected to be the same.
So this is why the example results are unexpected also in the degenerate case - the prior for everything else (the regression intercept and slope) are identical in the two cases.

But the data likelihoods are different, which will therefore also affect the other posteriors.
The difference in results are entirely expected.

In any case, my main concern was the problem with predicted values becoming numerically equal to 0 or 1 which appears to cause the crash.  This can easily occur if the response is always zero for some level of a factor in the model (or it can occur in less obvious ways involving some linear combination of covariates).  While parameter estimates obtained in such cases not necessarily can be trusted, it may still be of interest to fit an overparameterized model like this, for example, to assess goodness of fit of some simpler model.

For model+data such that the posterior mode is degenerate, there is a practical limitation to what can reasonably be expected from a general purpose numerical method.  Where you say that the predicted values become equal to 0 or 1, that's due to the linear predictor becoming close to - or + infinity, and handling that cleanly is non-trivial.  Mathematical theory and numerical reality don't always play well together.  Probably the only thing that can be done is to make sure that values are truncated before being fed into the beta-function, and hoping that that doesn't break something else.

Finn L

messages.author: a38e579a8decc4d1
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] betabinomial and linear separation
parts:
kl. 20:44:54 UTC+1 torsdag 27. november 2014 skrev Finn Lindgren følgende:
For model+data such that the posterior mode is degenerate, there is a practical limitation to what can reasonably be expected from a general purpose numerical method.  Where you say that the predicted values become equal to 0 or 1, that's due to the linear predictor becoming close to - or + infinity, and handling that cleanly is non-trivial.  Mathematical theory and numerical reality don't always play well together.  Probably the only thing that can be done is to make sure that values are truncated before being fed into the beta-function, and hoping that that doesn't break something else.

Consider this simpler case for which the ML is not degenerate which also provokes the error:

x <- c(1:4,40)
y <- c(0,1,0,2,2)
plot(x,y)
inla(y ~ x,family="betabinomial",data=data.frame(y,x),Ntrials=2)

There should be nothing particularly difficult or degenerate with the posterior in this case, near the posterior mode which is determined mostly by observations 1 to 4, the observation at x=40 contributes almost nothing to the log likelihood because this observation has probability very close to one (unless we are very far from the mode).  The problem is that its fitted value becomes numerically equal to 1 which makes things break since you don't check for this special case, see line numbers 5468-5484 at  

https://code.google.com/p/inla/source/browse/inlaprog/src/inla.c

resulting in a call to gsl_sf_lnbeta with the second argument equal to zero (as far as I can tell). I believe you can safely set the contribution to the log likelihood equal to 0 for such cases.

Jarle
